items.readable_text:
Content:
Line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] often come in pairs. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.]

Content:
We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.]

Content:
Let's evaluate this integral in this case where [MATH: C] is given by the line segment

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].]

Content:
Along the path [MATH: C,] we have

Content:
[MATH: x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.]

Content:
Computing the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t),] we get

Content:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(6t + 1)i + (d)/(dt)(2t + 1)j; = 6i + 2j.]

Content:
Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)(x + y)dx + (x − y)dy|= ∫_{0}^{1}(x + y) ⋅ (dx)/(dt)dt + (x − y) ⋅ (dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}((x + y) ⋅ (dx)/(dt) + (x − y) ⋅ (dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(6t + 1 + 2t + 1) ⋅ 6 + (6t + 1 − (2t + 1)) ⋅ 2dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(8t + 2) ⋅ 6 + (4t) ⋅ 2dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}48t + 12 + 8tdt; = ∫_{0}^{1}56t + 12dt; = 28t^{2} + 12t|_{0}^{1}; = 28 + 12; = 40.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Along the curve, we have [MATH: x(t) = t, \qquad y(t) = t^2.]

The derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t^{2})j; = i + 2tj.]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)(x^{2} + y)dx + xdy|= ∫_{0}^{1}(x^{2} + y)(dx)/(dt)dt + x(dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}((x^{2} + y)(dx)/(dt) + x(dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(t^{2} + t^{2}) ⋅ 1 + t ⋅ 2tdt; = ∫_{0}^{1}2t^{2} + 2t^{2}dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{2}dt; = 4∫_{0}^{1}t^{2}dt]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y,z)] be a function of three variables and [MATH: C] be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz]

Content:
For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy + f \, \textrm dz]

Content:
As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve [MATH: C] using the parameter [MATH: t\in [a,b]] and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)fdx + fdy + fdz|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(dx)/(dt)dt + f(dy)/(dt)dt + f(dz)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(f(dx)/(dt) + f(dy)/(dt) + f(dz)/(dt))dt]

Content:
Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.]

Content:
Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f x'+ f y' + f z' \,\textrm d t,]

Content:
where the primes denote differentiation with respect to [MATH: t.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Along the curve, we have [MATH: x(t) =2t, \qquad y(t) = \cos t , \qquad z(t) = \sin t.]

The derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j + (dz)/(dt)k; = (d)/(dt)(2t)i + (d)/(dt)(\cos t)j + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)k; = 2i − \sin tj + \cos tk.]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)x^{3}dx + zdy + ydz|= ∫_{0}^{π}x^{3}(dx)/(dt)dt + z(dy)/(dt)dt + y(dz)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}(x^{3}(dx)/(dt) + z(dy)/(dt) + y(dz)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}(2t)^{3} ⋅ (2) + \sin t ⋅ (− \sin t) + \cos t ⋅ (\cos t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} − \sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} tdt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} + (\cos^{2} t − \sin^{2} t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} + \cos 2tdt]

sections.normalized_html: Evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x -x\,\mathrm{d}y ,] where [MATH: C] is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}] for [MATH: t\in[0,\pi].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Along the curve, we have [MATH: x(t) = \cos t, \qquad y(t) = 3\sin t.]

The derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(\cos t)i + (d)/(dt)(3\sin t)j; = − \sin ti + 3\cos tj.]

We can now evaluate the line integral:

[MATH: ∫_(C)ydx − xdy|= ∫_{0}^{π}y ⋅ (dx)/(dt)dt − x ⋅ (dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}(y ⋅ (dx)/(dt) − x ⋅ (dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}3\sin t ⋅ (− \sin t) − (\cos t) ⋅ 3\cos tdt; = ∫_{0}^{π} − 3\sin^{2} t − 3\cos^{2} tdt; = − 3∫_{0}^{π}\sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} tdt; = − 3∫_{0}^{π}dt; = − 3t|_{0}^{π}; = − 3π]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] often come in pairs. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.]

Content:
We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.]

Content:
Let's evaluate this integral in this case where [MATH: C] is given by the line segment

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].]

Content:
Along the path [MATH: C,] we have

Content:
[MATH: x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.]

Content:
Computing the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t),] we get

Content:
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(6t + 1)i + (d)/(dt)(2t + 1)j; = 6i + 2j.]

Content:
Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)(x + y)dx + (x − y)dy|= ∫_{0}^{1}(x + y) ⋅ (dx)/(dt)dt + (x − y) ⋅ (dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}((x + y) ⋅ (dx)/(dt) + (x − y) ⋅ (dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(6t + 1 + 2t + 1) ⋅ 6 + (6t + 1 − (2t + 1)) ⋅ 2dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(8t + 2) ⋅ 6 + (4t) ⋅ 2dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}48t + 12 + 8tdt; = ∫_{0}^{1}56t + 12dt; = 28t^{2} + 12t|_{0}^{1}; = 28 + 12; = 40.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

Example Prompt:
Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,] where [MATH: C] is parametrized by [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}] for [MATH: t\in\left[0,1\right].]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Along the curve, we have
[MATH: x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.]

The derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j; = (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t^{2})j; = i + 2tj.]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)(x^{2} + y)dx + xdy|= ∫_{0}^{1}(x^{2} + y)(dx)/(dt)dt + x(dy)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}((x^{2} + y)(dx)/(dt) + x(dy)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}(t^{2} + t^{2}) ⋅ 1 + t ⋅ 2tdt; = ∫_{0}^{1}2t^{2} + 2t^{2}dt; = ∫_{0}^{1}4t^{2}dt; = 4∫_{0}^{1}t^{2}dt]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

Content:
Let [MATH: f(x,y,z)] be a function of three variables and [MATH: C] be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz]

Content:
For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy + f \, \textrm dz]

Content:
As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve [MATH: C] using the parameter [MATH: t\in [a,b]] and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_(C)fdx + fdy + fdz|= ∫_{a}^{b}f(dx)/(dt)dt + f(dy)/(dt)dt + f(dz)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{a}^{b}(f(dx)/(dt) + f(dy)/(dt) + f(dz)/(dt))dt]

Content:
Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.]

Content:
Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

Content:
[MATH: \int_a^b f x'+ f y' + f z' \,\textrm d t,]

Content:
where the primes denote differentiation with respect to [MATH: t.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

Example Prompt:
Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to [MATH: \displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,] where [MATH: C] is a portion of the helix [MATH: \mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}] for [MATH: t\in[0,\pi]?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Along the curve, we have
[MATH: x(t) =2t, \qquad
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad
z(t) = \sin t.]

The derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] is given by

[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (dx)/(dt)i + (dy)/(dt)j + (dz)/(dt)k; = (d)/(dt)(2t)i + (d)/(dt)(\cos t)j + (d)/(dt)(\sin t)k; = 2i − \sin tj + \cos tk.]

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

[MATH: ∫_(C)x^{3}dx + zdy + ydz|= ∫_{0}^{π}x^{3}(dx)/(dt)dt + z(dy)/(dt)dt + y(dz)/(dt)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}(x^{3}(dx)/(dt) + z(dy)/(dt) + y(dz)/(dt))dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}(2t)^{3} ⋅ (2) + \sin t ⋅ (− \sin t) + \cos t ⋅ (\cos t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} − \sin^{2} t + \cos^{2} tdt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} + (\cos^{2} t − \sin^{2} t)dt; = ∫_{0}^{π}16t^{3} + \cos 2tdt]
